questions.knowledge_point: Multiplying a Matrix by the Identity Matrix
questions.problem:
Calculate the product ${I}_{2}B$ given that ${I}_{2}$ is the $2\times 2$ identity matrix and
$B=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Any matrix, when multiplied by an identity matrix, remains unchanged (assuming that the multiplication is well defined).

The matrix ${I}_{2}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $B$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix too. 

Therefore, the multiplication is well defined and 

$$
{I}_{2}\cdot B=B=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Multiplying a Matrix by a Column or Row of the Identity Matrix
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $B$ is the $2$nd *column* of the identity matrix ${I}_{3}.$

Since we're multiplying the $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ by the $2$nd *column* of the identity matrix ${I}_{3},$ the result must be the $2$nd *column* of $A.$ Therefore,

$$
AB=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Let's check the long way:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 0+(\frac{-\sqrt{2}}{2})\cdot 1+0\cdot 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 0+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 1+0\cdot 0 \\ 0\cdot 0+0\cdot 1+1\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $B$ is the $1$st *column* of the identity matrix ${I}_{3}.$

Since we're multiplying the $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ by the $1$st *column* of the identity matrix ${I}_{3},$ the result must be the $1$st *column* of $A.$ Therefore,

$$
AB=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{7} \\ -2 \\ \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Let's check the long way:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{7} & -3 & 3.5 \\ -2 & 2\sqrt{5} & -2.5 \\ \sqrt{3} & 4 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{7}\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot 0+3.5\cdot 0 \\ (-2)\cdot 1+2\sqrt{5}\cdot 0+(-2.5)\cdot 0 \\ \sqrt{3}\cdot 1+4\cdot 0+5\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{7} \\ -2 \\ \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Multiplying a Matrix by a Column or Row of the Identity Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate the product $C D,$ if
$[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -4 \\ 5 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}]$
and 
$[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $D$ is the $2$nd *column* of the identity matrix $I_3.$

Since we're multiplying the $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ by the $2$nd *column* of the identity matrix $I_3,$ the result must be the $2$nd *column* of $C.$ Therefore,

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Don't believe it? Let's check the long way:

$$
\begin{aligned}CD & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -4 \\ 5 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+0\cdot 0 \\ -1\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+(-4)\cdot 0 \\ 5\cdot 0+4\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
